Recall the graph of the function [MATH: y=\cot x\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:

Content:
Similarly to the tangent, the cotangent has infinitely many zeros, and the function has an infinite number of vertical asymptotes.
Let's construct general expressions for these, assuming that [MATH: n] represents an integer.

Content:
The Zeros of the Function

Content:
From the graph, the function has a zero when [MATH: x=\dfrac\pi 2,] and the function is periodic with period [MATH: \pi.] Therefore, a general expression for the zeros is

Content:
[MATH: x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}+ n\pi.]

Content:
The Vertical Asymptotes of the Function

Content:
From the graph, we see that the vertical asymptotes of the function occur at [MATH: x=0,\pm\pi,\pm2\pi,\dots.]

Content:
Therefore, a general equation for the asymptotes is

Content:
[MATH: x = n\pi.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's plot the graph of [MATH: y=\cot x.]

Now, let's go through each statement.

  • Statement I is false. The zeros of the function occur at the values [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+n\pi.]

  • Statement II is false. The vertical asymptotes of the function are at integer multiples of [MATH: \pi], i.e., [MATH: x=n\pi.]

  • Statement III is false. The range of [MATH: y=\cot x] is [MATH: (-\infty, \infty).]

In conclusion, none of the statements are true.

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \cot x = 1] for some [MATH: x,] then find the value of [MATH: \cot(x+5\pi).]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \cot x = 1] for some [MATH: x,] then find the value of [MATH: \cot(x+5\pi).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The period of [MATH: y = \cot x] is [MATH: \pi.] Therefore, for any integer [MATH: n,] we have

[MATH: \cot{x} = \cot{(x+n\pi)} .]

Substituting [MATH: n=5] into the above gives

[MATH: \cot x|= \cot (x + 5 ⋅ π); = \cot (x + 5π).]

Therefore, if [MATH: \cot{x} = 1,] then [MATH: \cot{(x+5\pi)} = 1.]

Content:
Recall that a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if it satisfies the property

Content:
[MATH: f(-x) = -f(x).]

Content:
As it turns out, cotangent is an odd function! So, for any value of [MATH: x,] we have
[MATH: \cot(-x) = -\cot(x).]

Content:
Odd functions always have rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This is indeed true of the cotangent function, as we can see from the diagram below.

Graphic:

items.title: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Cotangent Function

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \cot x = 2,] then what is the value of [MATH: \cot (-x+7\pi)?]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \cot x = 2,] then what is the value of [MATH: \cot (-x+7\pi)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y=\cot{x}.]

From the graph, we note the following:

  • The period of [MATH: \cot{x}] is [MATH: \pi.]

  • Our graph has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This means that [MATH: \cot{x}] is an odd function, and we have [MATH: \cot(-x) = -\cot{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

  • Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \cot{x},] we have [MATH: \cot (− x + 7π)|= \cot (− x + π ⋅ 7); = \cot (− x).]

  • Secondly, using the oddness of [MATH: \cot{x},] we have [MATH: \cot (− x)|= − \cot x; = − 2.]

Therefore, [MATH: \cot (-x+7\pi)=-2.]

Item 10 — Example: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Cotangent Function

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: \cot x = 2,] then what is the value of [MATH: \cot (-x+7\pi)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y=\cot{x}.]

[IMG: /graphics/bab1cfa649007237d6c54ebc22aa3e68]

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of [MATH: \cot{x}] is [MATH: \pi.]
- Our graph has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This means that [MATH: \cot{x}] is an odd function, and we have
[MATH: \cot(-x) = -\cot{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \cot{x},] we have
[MATH: \cot (− x + 7π)|= \cot (− x + π ⋅ 7); = \cot (− x).]
- Secondly, using the oddness of [MATH: \cot{x},] we have
[MATH: \cot (− x)|= − \cot x; = − 2.]

Therefore, [MATH: \cot (-x+7\pi)=-2.]
